aspirin.name: Aspirin
aspirin.summary: A low-dose antiplatelet that stops platelets clumping into clots, used long term after heart attacks and strokes; at higher doses it is a painkiller and anti-inflammatory.
usedFor: Preventing further heart attacks and strokes in people who have had one (secondary prevention)
During a suspected heart attack (300 mg chewed) and after stents
Pain, fever and inflammation at higher doses (now largely replaced by ibuprofen and paracetamol)
Pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk pregnancy
aspirin.howItWorks: Irreversibly blocks the enzyme COX-1 in platelets so they cannot make thromboxane, the signal that makes them clump. Because platelets have no nucleus they cannot make new enzyme, so one small daily dose keeps them quiet for their whole 7-10 day life. Higher doses also block COX-2 in tissues, reducing prostaglandins that cause pain, fever and inflammation.
forms: Tablets 75 mg (dispersible or enteric coated), 300 mg
aspirin.onset: Antiplatelet effect within an hour of a chewed dose; lasts the life of the platelet.

common: Indigestion, stomach irritation

serious: Stomach ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding (risk rises with age, alcohol, NSAIDs and anticoagulants)

aspirin.understand: A small daily dose of aspirin stops platelets, the tiny cell fragments that start clots, from sticking together. That makes a clot in a narrowed heart or brain artery less likely, which is why it is taken after a heart attack or stroke. Bigger doses also block the chemicals that cause pain, fever and inflammation.
aspirin.mechanismDetail: Aspirin acetylates a serine residue in the active site of cyclo-oxygenase, inhibiting it irreversibly. In platelets, which cannot synthesise new enzyme, this abolishes thromboxane A2 production for the platelet's lifespan (7-10 days), reducing aggregation; because the effect is irreversible, a single low daily dose (75-100 mg) is enough and the effect persists for days after stopping. At analgesic doses (300-900 mg) aspirin also inhibits COX-2 in inflamed tissue and the hypothalamus, reducing prostaglandin-mediated pain sensitisation, inflammation and fever. Inhibition of gastric COX-1 removes the prostaglandins that protect the mucosa, the basis of dyspepsia, ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding; reduced renal prostaglandins can impair kidney perfusion. Aspirin is rapidly hydrolysed to salicylate, which is the main circulating species at higher doses.

ibuprofen.name: Ibuprofen
ibuprofen.summary: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) that eases pain, inflammation and fever by blocking prostaglandin production; effective but hard on the stomach and kidneys if overused.
usedFor: Pain with an inflammatory component: sprains, back pain, period pain, dental pain, headache
Arthritis flares and gout attacks (short courses)
Fever
Relatives: naproxen (longer acting), diclofenac, and the COX-2-selective celecoxib and etoricoxib
ibuprofen.howItWorks: Blocks the cyclo-oxygenase enzymes COX-1 and COX-2, cutting production of prostaglandins, the local messengers that sensitise pain nerves, widen vessels in inflamed tissue and reset the brain's thermostat in fever. The same prostaglandins protect the stomach lining and keep blood flowing through the kidneys, which explains the main harms.
forms: Tablets 200-400 mg, liquid for children, topical gel for local joint and muscle pain (fewer side effects)

common: Indigestion, nausea
Fluid retention, raised blood pressure
serious: Stomach and duodenal ulcers with bleeding or perforation, especially over 65, with steroids, aspirin or anticoagulants
Acute kidney injury, particularly when dehydrated or with ACE inhibitors and diuretics ('triple whammy')
Heart attack and stroke risk rises with high doses and prolonged use, most with diclofenac and COX-2 inhibitors

ibuprofen.understand: Ibuprofen blocks the enzymes that make prostaglandins, the chemical messengers that make injured tissue painful, swollen and hot and that raise your temperature in fever. With fewer prostaglandins there is less pain, swelling and fever. The same messengers protect the stomach and keep blood flowing to the kidneys, which is why ibuprofen can upset the stomach and strain the kidneys.
ibuprofen.mechanismDetail: Ibuprofen is a propionic acid NSAID that reversibly and non-selectively inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, reducing synthesis of prostaglandins and thromboxane from arachidonic acid. COX-2 inhibition at sites of inflammation reduces PGE2-mediated nociceptor sensitisation, vasodilation and oedema, and central COX inhibition lowers the hypothalamic set-point in fever. COX-1 inhibition in the gastric mucosa reduces protective mucus and bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow (dyspepsia, ulceration, bleeding), in the kidney reduces the prostaglandins that maintain afferent arteriolar dilatation when renal perfusion is threatened (acute kidney injury in dehydration or with ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics), and in platelets transiently impairs aggregation. Ibuprofen occupying platelet COX-1 can also block the access of aspirin to its acetylation site, blunting aspirin's cardioprotective effect when the two are taken together. All NSAIDs carry a dose- and duration-related increase in thrombotic cardiovascular events; ibuprofen at 1200 mg daily or less appears to carry the lowest risk.

paracetamol.name: Paracetamol
paracetamol.summary: The first-line painkiller and fever reducer for most people (acetaminophen in North America), gentle on the stomach at normal doses but toxic to the liver in overdose.
usedFor: Mild to moderate pain of any cause: headache, muscle aches, back pain, osteoarthritis, after surgery
Fever
First-line pain relief in pregnancy and for children (by weight)
Combined with opioids (co-codamol) or given intravenously in hospital
paracetamol.howItWorks: Still not fully understood. It weakly inhibits cyclo-oxygenase in the brain and spinal cord rather than in inflamed tissue, and its breakdown product AM404 acts on cannabinoid and TRPV1 pathways in the central nervous system, raising the pain threshold and lowering the fever set-point. It has almost no anti-inflammatory effect and does not irritate the stomach.
forms: Tablets and capsules 500 mg, soluble tablets, liquid, suppositories, intravenous infusion
paracetamol.onset: 30-60 minutes orally; lasts 4-6 hours. Maximum 4 g in 24 hours for adults (less if under 50 kg or with liver disease).

common: Very few at normal doses; occasional rash
serious: Liver failure in overdose: even 8-10 g (16-20 tablets) can be fatal without treatment, and the danger rises with alcohol, malnutrition and enzyme-inducing drugs
Rare severe skin reactions and blood disorders

paracetamol.understand: Paracetamol eases pain and lowers fever by acting mainly in the brain and spinal cord, where it raises the threshold at which pain is felt and resets the body's thermostat. It does little against inflammation and does not irritate the stomach, which is why it is the first painkiller tried for most people, but too much of it damages the liver.
paracetamol.mechanismDetail: Paracetamol's mechanism is incompletely defined. It inhibits cyclo-oxygenase in the central nervous system, where peroxide levels are low, more than in inflamed peripheral tissue, which explains analgesia and antipyresis without meaningful anti-inflammatory or antiplatelet activity. Its metabolite AM404, formed in the brain from p-aminophenol, activates TRPV1 and cannabinoid CB1 pathways and reinforces descending serotonergic inhibition of pain. At therapeutic doses it is conjugated by glucuronidation and sulphation; a small fraction is oxidised by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which is detoxified by glutathione. In overdose, glutathione is exhausted and NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is most effective within 8 hours. Chronic alcohol use, malnutrition, low body weight and enzyme-inducing drugs increase susceptibility.

morphine.name: Morphine and opioids
morphine.summary: The reference strong opioid for severe pain, such as after major surgery, injury or in advanced cancer; highly effective but sedating, constipating and able to slow breathing.
usedFor: Severe acute pain: heart attack, fractures, after major surgery, sickle cell crises

morphine.howItWorks: Binds mu-opioid receptors on nerve cells in the spinal cord, brainstem and brain, the same receptors used by the body's own endorphins. This closes the gate on pain signals entering the spinal cord, dampens the emotional response to pain in the brain and, unwantedly, slows the breathing centre in the brainstem, slows the gut and triggers nausea and euphoria.
forms: Immediate-release oral liquid and tablets, 12-hourly modified-release tablets, injections into vein, muscle or under the skin, patient-controlled pumps, patches (fentanyl, buprenorphine)
morphine.onset: Intravenous within minutes; oral 30-60 minutes; modified-release over hours.

Falls and confusion in the elderly; hormone suppression and immune effects long term
Opioid-induced hyperalgesia: pain becoming worse with escalating doses

Never crush or chew modified-release forms

atorvastatin.name: Atorvastatin
atorvastatin.summary: A high-intensity statin that lowers LDL cholesterol by blocking its production in the liver, cutting the risk of heart attack and stroke in people at raised cardiovascular risk.
usedFor: Lowering LDL cholesterol to prevent heart attacks and strokes
Everyone with established cardiovascular disease (secondary prevention, usually 80 mg)
Primary prevention when 10-year cardiovascular risk is 10% or more, in diabetes, chronic kidney disease and familial hypercholesterolaemia (usually 20 mg)
atorvastatin.howItWorks: Blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. The liver responds by putting more LDL receptors on its surface to pull cholesterol out of the blood, so LDL falls by 40-55%. Statins also stabilise the fatty plaques in artery walls, making them less likely to rupture and cause a clot.
forms: Tablets 10, 20, 40, 80 mg, once daily at any time (simvastatin at night)
atorvastatin.onset: Cholesterol falls within two weeks; plaque benefits build over years. Taken lifelong.

serious: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown, very rare), more with high doses, interacting drugs and hypothyroidism

Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; active liver disease
Unexplained muscle pain with dark urine needs a same-day creatine kinase test

atorvastatin.monitoring: Lipids and liver tests at baseline, 3 months and 12 months; creatine kinase only if muscle symptoms.

atorvastatin.understand: Atorvastatin blocks an enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. The liver responds by pulling more LDL ('bad') cholesterol out of the blood, so less is deposited in artery walls and the risk of heart attack and stroke falls.
atorvastatin.mechanismDetail: Atorvastatin is a competitive, reversible inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Lower intracellular cholesterol activates SREBP-2, which increases LDL-receptor expression on hepatocytes, so LDL and VLDL remnants are cleared from plasma faster; LDL cholesterol falls by about 40-55% depending on dose (high-intensity at 40-80 mg), with modest reductions in triglycerides and a small rise in HDL. Beyond lipids, statins reduce inflammation in plaques and improve endothelial function, contributing to plaque stabilisation. Atorvastatin is metabolised by CYP3A4, so strong inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, ciclosporin, some HIV protease inhibitors, large amounts of grapefruit juice) raise exposure and myopathy risk. Its active metabolites give a long duration of effect, allowing dosing at any time of day.

ramipril.name: Ramipril
ramipril.summary: An ACE inhibitor that relaxes blood vessels and eases the heart's workload, used for high blood pressure, heart failure, after heart attacks and to protect the kidneys in diabetes.
usedFor: High blood pressure (first choice under 55 and in diabetes)
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (improves survival)
After a heart attack
Protecting the kidneys in diabetes and chronic kidney disease with protein in the urine
Angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan, candesartan) do the same job for people who cough on ACE inhibitors
ramipril.howItWorks: Blocks the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, the hormone that constricts arteries, drives the adrenal glands to release aldosterone (salt and water retention) and thickens heart muscle and vessel walls. Less angiotensin II means relaxed vessels, lower pressure, less strain on a failing heart and lower pressure inside the kidney's filters. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, which accumulates and causes the characteristic dry cough.
forms: Capsules and tablets 1.25-10 mg once daily
ramipril.onset: Blood pressure falls within hours; full effect in a few weeks. Started low and titrated.

common: Dry tickly cough (10-15%, from bradykinin)
Dizziness with the first doses, tiredness, headache
A small rise in creatinine and potassium
serious: Angio-oedema: swelling of the lips, tongue and throat, can block the airway; stop immediately
Acute kidney injury when dehydrated, on NSAIDs, or with narrowed renal arteries
High potassium, especially with spironolactone, kidney disease or potassium supplements
Harm to the fetus: stop before or as soon as pregnancy is known

cautions: Pause on 'sick days' with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever to protect the kidneys
Avoid with NSAIDs and potassium supplements; caution with diuretics (first-dose hypotension)
Bilateral renal artery stenosis, previous angio-oedema, pregnancy: do not use
ramipril.monitoring: Kidney function and potassium before starting, 1-2 weeks after each dose change, then yearly; blood pressure.

metoprolol.name: Metoprolol and beta blockers
metoprolol.summary: A beta blocker that slows the heart and reduces its oxygen demand, used for angina, after heart attacks, in heart failure and to control fast heart rhythms.
usedFor: Angina and after a heart attack (reduce the heart's oxygen demand and the risk of dangerous rhythms)
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (bisoprolol, carvedilol: improve survival when started low and slow)
Controlling the rate in atrial fibrillation and other fast rhythms
High blood pressure (no longer first line unless another indication)
Propranolol for migraine prevention, tremor, anxiety symptoms and thyroid storm
metoprolol.howItWorks: Occupies beta-1 receptors on heart muscle and the conducting system so adrenaline and noradrenaline cannot stimulate them. The heart beats more slowly and less forcefully, uses less oxygen, and the AV node lets fewer atrial impulses through. Non-selective agents (propranolol) also block beta-2 receptors in airways and blood vessels, which is why they can trigger asthma.
forms: Tablets (metoprolol 25-100 mg twice daily or modified release once daily; bisoprolol 1.25-10 mg once daily); intravenous for rapid rate control
metoprolol.onset: Heart rate falls within an hour; heart failure benefit builds over months.

common: Tiredness, cold hands and feet, slow pulse
Dizziness on standing, vivid dreams, sleep disturbance
Erectile dysfunction
Masking the warning signs of low blood sugar in diabetes
serious: Severe bradycardia or heart block
Worsening of heart failure if started at too high a dose
Bronchospasm in asthma (especially non-selective agents)
Rebound angina, fast rhythms or blood pressure surge if stopped abruptly

cautions: Never stop suddenly: taper over one to two weeks
Asthma (relative contraindication), severe peripheral arterial disease, uncontrolled heart failure, second- or third-degree heart block
Caution with verapamil and diltiazem (additive slowing), and in diabetes
metoprolol.monitoring: Pulse and blood pressure; ECG if the rate falls below 50 or symptoms occur.

amlodipine.name: Amlodipine
amlodipine.summary: A long-acting calcium channel blocker that relaxes artery walls to lower blood pressure and prevent angina, taken once daily and among the most prescribed medicines worldwide.
usedFor: High blood pressure (first choice over 55 and in people of Black African or Caribbean origin, or when an ACE inhibitor is not suitable)
Angina prevention
Non-dihydropyridine relatives (diltiazem, verapamil) also slow the heart and treat some fast rhythms
amlodipine.howItWorks: Blocks L-type calcium channels in the smooth muscle of artery walls. Muscle cells need calcium to contract, so with fewer channels open the arteries relax and widen, lowering resistance and blood pressure and letting more blood reach heart muscle. Amlodipine selects vessels over heart muscle, so it does not slow the heart; its long half-life gives smooth 24-hour control.
forms: Tablets 5 or 10 mg once daily
amlodipine.onset: Gradual, over days; steady state in about a week.

common: Ankle swelling (fluid leaking from widened capillaries, not heart failure; not helped by diuretics)
Flushing, headache, palpitations in the first weeks
Gum overgrowth, tiredness, dizziness
serious: Marked low blood pressure with fainting, particularly with other blood-pressure medicines or dehydration
Chest pain that is new or worse in the first days of treatment (rare reflex tachycardia)
Allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips or throat, difficulty breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (rare liver reaction)

cautions: Grapefruit juice increases levels of some calcium channel blockers
Severe aortic stenosis, cardiogenic shock, unstable angina
Simvastatin dose is limited with amlodipine
amlodipine.monitoring: Blood pressure; no blood tests needed for amlodipine.

amlodipine.understand: Amlodipine relaxes the muscle in the walls of your arteries so that they widen. Blood flows through them with less resistance, which lowers blood pressure and lets more blood reach the heart muscle, which helps prevent angina.
amlodipine.mechanismDetail: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine that binds the alpha-1 subunit of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, preferring the inactivated channel state that predominates in depolarised arterial muscle. Reduced calcium influx lowers activation of myosin light-chain kinase, so arteriolar tone and total peripheral resistance fall while cardiac contractility and sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction are little affected at therapeutic doses (in contrast to verapamil and diltiazem). Coronary arteries and arterioles dilate, improving oxygen delivery in chronic stable and vasospastic angina. The slow onset and long elimination half-life (35-50 hours) give gradual, sustained 24-hour blood-pressure control without reflex tachycardia.

indications.note: Prophylaxis of chronic stable angina and vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina

warnings.text: Amlodipine may be prescribed with care, or a different medicine chosen, for people with severe heart failure, because dihydropyridines can worsen fluid retention in some patients; the BNF lists heart failure among its cautions.

Amlodipine is cleared by the liver; in hepatic impairment the half-life is prolonged and a lower starting dose is advised, with slow titration in severe impairment.

Ankle swelling is a dose-related effect of dihydropyridines caused by widened capillaries, not by heart failure, and does not respond to diuretics; it is a reason to review the dose rather than to add a water tablet.

furosemide.name: Furosemide
furosemide.summary: A powerful loop diuretic that makes the kidneys excrete salt and water within an hour, used to clear fluid overload in heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease.
usedFor: Fluid overload in heart failure: breathlessness, swollen legs, fluid on the lungs (intravenous in emergencies)
Oedema from kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome) and liver cirrhosis (with spironolactone)
High blood pressure when kidney function is poor
Thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide, bendroflumethiazide) are the gentler relatives used for blood pressure
furosemide.howItWorks: Blocks the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the segment that reabsorbs a quarter of all filtered sodium. Salt that stays in the tubule drags water with it, so urine output can rise several-fold within an hour. Potassium, magnesium and calcium are lost too, and the kidney compensates by activating the renin-angiotensin system.
forms: Tablets 20, 40, 500 mg; oral solution; intravenous injection or infusion
furosemide.onset: Oral within an hour, lasting about 6 hours (hence the name Lasix: 'lasts six'); intravenous within minutes.

common: Passing lots of urine, urgency (take in the morning)
Dizziness on standing, dehydration, thirst, cramps
Low potassium, sodium and magnesium; raised uric acid (gout) and glucose
serious: Acute kidney injury from over-diuresis
Dangerous potassium or sodium disturbance and arrhythmia
Hearing loss (ototoxicity) with rapid high intravenous doses, especially with aminoglycosides
Collapse from low blood pressure in the frail

cautions: Daily weights in heart failure guide the dose: a gain of 2 kg in 3 days often means more diuretic
Pause on sick days with vomiting or diarrhoea
Care with lithium, digoxin, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides
Severe low potassium or sodium, anuria, dehydration: do not use until corrected
furosemide.monitoring: Kidney function and electrolytes within a week of starting or changing dose, then regularly; weight and blood pressure.

glyceryl-trinitrate.name: Glyceryl trinitrate
glyceryl-trinitrate.summary: A fast-acting nitrate spray or tablet under the tongue that widens veins and coronary arteries to relieve an angina attack within minutes.
usedFor: Relieving an angina attack within minutes (spray or tablet under the tongue)
Preventing angina before exertion
Intravenous infusion for unstable angina, heart attack with ongoing pain and acute heart failure
Long-acting isosorbide mononitrate for regular angina prevention; GTN ointment for anal fissures
glyceryl-trinitrate.howItWorks: Releases nitric oxide in vascular smooth muscle, activating guanylate cyclase and relaxing the vessel. Veins dilate most, so less blood returns to the heart and it has less to pump against (lower preload and wall tension, lower oxygen demand); coronary arteries and collaterals widen, improving supply to ischaemic muscle. Relief within one to three minutes helps confirm that chest pain was angina, though oesophageal spasm responds too.
forms: Sublingual spray 400 micrograms per dose or tablets; patches; intravenous infusion; modified-release tablets (isosorbide)

common: Throbbing headache (from dilated scalp vessels), flushing
Dizziness and faintness from a drop in blood pressure: sit down before using
serious: Severe hypotension and collapse if combined with sildenafil or similar drugs (contraindicated within 24-48 hours)
Fast heart rate; rarely worsening of angina; methaemoglobinaemia with prolonged infusion

cautions: Tolerance develops with continuous exposure: long-acting nitrates need a nitrate-free interval each day
If pain persists 5 minutes after a second dose, call emergency services: it may be a heart attack
Severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, very low blood pressure, raised intracranial pressure
Tablets lose potency after 8 weeks once opened; sprays last longer
glyceryl-trinitrate.monitoring: Blood pressure during infusions; frequency of spray use is a marker of angina control.

apixaban.name: Apixaban and DOACs
apixaban.summary: A direct oral anticoagulant that blocks clotting factor Xa, preventing strokes in atrial fibrillation and treating deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism without routine blood monitoring.
usedFor: Preventing stroke in atrial fibrillation (first choice over warfarin for most)
Treating and preventing deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Preventing clots after hip and knee replacement
Not used for mechanical heart valves or antiphospholipid syndrome (warfarin remains)
apixaban.howItWorks: Binds directly to activated factor X, the enzyme at the junction of the clotting cascade that converts prothrombin to thrombin. Less thrombin means less fibrin, so clots that form in the slow-flowing left atrial appendage or leg veins are prevented or stopped from growing. Unlike warfarin the effect is predictable, starts within hours, needs no blood-level monitoring and is little affected by diet.
forms: Tablets 2.5 or 5 mg twice daily (rivaroxaban and edoxaban once daily)
apixaban.onset: Peak effect 3-4 hours after a dose; wears off within a day or two of stopping.

common: Bruising, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, heavier periods
Nausea, anaemia
serious: Major bleeding: gastrointestinal, intracranial (about half the rate of warfarin), retroperitoneal
Bleeding after trauma or surgery; reversal agents (andexanet, idarucizumab for dabigatran) exist but are limited
Spinal haematoma with epidural anaesthesia

cautions: Dose reduced with kidney impairment, low weight, age over 80 (apixaban), and some interacting drugs
Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless specifically advised; alcohol in moderation
Stop 24-72 hours before surgery depending on bleeding risk and kidney function
Missed doses matter because the effect wears off quickly; do not double up
apixaban.monitoring: Kidney function, blood count and weight at least yearly (more often if kidney function is poor); no INR needed.

warfarin.name: Warfarin
warfarin.summary: The long-established oral anticoagulant that blocks vitamin K-dependent clotting factors; effective for mechanical heart valves and clots but needs regular INR blood tests and careful dosing.
usedFor: Mechanical heart valves (the only oral anticoagulant licensed)
Atrial fibrillation with moderate or severe mitral stenosis, and antiphospholipid syndrome
Venous thromboembolism where DOACs are unsuitable (severe kidney failure, cost)
Historically the standard anticoagulant, now largely replaced by DOACs for other indications
warfarin.howItWorks: Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase in the liver, so vitamin K cannot be recycled to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Existing factors take days to be cleared, so the effect starts after 2-3 days and heparin cover is needed for immediate protection. The dose needed varies enormously between people and with diet, illness and other drugs, so the INR blood test tunes it.
forms: Tablets 0.5, 1, 3 and 5 mg (colour-coded), taken once daily at the same time
warfarin.onset: Therapeutic after 3-5 days; effect persists 3-5 days after stopping. Reversed with vitamin K (slow) or prothrombin complex concentrate (immediate).

common: Bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds
Hair thinning, rash
serious: Major bleeding, including intracranial: risk rises steeply when the INR is above 4
Skin necrosis in the first days (protein C deficiency), purple toe syndrome
Fetal harm: teratogenic in the first trimester and bleeding later

Keep vitamin K intake steady rather than avoiding it
Carry an anticoagulant alert card; tell dentists and pharmacists

metformin.name: Metformin
metformin.summary: The first-line tablet for type 2 diabetes: it reduces the glucose the liver releases and improves the body's response to insulin, without causing low blood sugar on its own.
usedFor: First-line drug for type 2 diabetes alongside diet and exercise
Prediabetes in people at high risk
Polycystic ovary syndrome (off label) and gestational diabetes
metformin.howItWorks: Reduces the amount of glucose the liver releases into blood (by inhibiting gluconeogenesis via AMP-activated protein kinase and the mitochondrial redox state), increases the sensitivity of muscle and fat to insulin, and modestly reduces glucose absorption from the gut. It does not stimulate insulin release, so it does not cause hypoglycaemia on its own or weight gain; HbA1c falls by about 11 mmol/mol (1%).
forms: Tablets 500 mg and 850 mg with meals, up to 2 g daily; modified-release once daily for those with gut side effects; oral solution
metformin.onset: Glucose lowering within days; full effect in 2-3 weeks. Started low and increased weekly.

common: Nausea, diarrhoea, bloating, metallic taste (a third at the start, most settle; take with food, build up slowly, or use modified release)
Vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
serious: Lactic acidosis: very rare, but dangerous when the drug accumulates in kidney failure, or in severe illness, dehydration, sepsis, heart failure or heavy alcohol use
Hypoglycaemia only when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas

cautions: Dose reduced when eGFR is below 45 and stopped below 30
Pause during acute illness with dehydration ('sick day rules') and around iodine contrast scans and surgery
Check B12 if anaemia, tingling or fatigue develop
Alcohol in moderation
metformin.monitoring: HbA1c every 3-6 months; kidney function at least yearly; B12 periodically.

NICE NG28: Type 2 diabetes in adults: management

routes: Oral (immediate-release and modified-release tablets, oral solution, powder sachets)
metformin.understand: Metformin lowers blood glucose mainly by telling the liver to release less sugar between meals, and by helping muscle respond to insulin. It does not make the pancreas release more insulin, so on its own it does not cause low blood sugar.
metformin.mechanismDetail: Metformin accumulates in hepatocytes via the OCT1 transporter and reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis: it lowers the mitochondrial energy state (partial inhibition of complex I and of mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase, shifting the cytosolic redox state) and activates AMP-activated protein kinase, which suppresses gluconeogenic gene expression and lipogenesis. Peripheral insulin sensitivity improves modestly, intestinal glucose uptake and GLP-1 secretion increase, and the gut microbiome changes. Because insulin secretion is not stimulated, hypoglycaemia does not occur with monotherapy and weight is neutral or slightly reduced. Metformin is not metabolised and is cleared by the kidney (tubular secretion); accumulation in renal failure, hypoxia or severe illness impairs lactate clearance and can precipitate lactic acidosis. It reduces ileal vitamin B12 absorption.

Less glucose released into the blood between meals

Alone or with other medicines and with diet and exercise

insulin.name: Insulin
insulin.summary: The hormone that moves glucose from the blood into cells, given by injection or pump to everyone with type 1 diabetes and to many with type 2 when other treatments are not enough.
usedFor: Type 1 diabetes: essential for life from diagnosis
Type 2 diabetes when tablets no longer control glucose, in pregnancy, and during severe illness or surgery
Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar states (intravenous infusion)
Lowering dangerously high potassium (with glucose) in emergencies
insulin.howItWorks: Replaces the hormone the pancreatic beta cells no longer make. Insulin binds receptors on muscle, fat and liver cells, moving GLUT4 transporters to the surface so glucose enters cells; it switches the liver from making glucose to storing glycogen, stops fat breakdown and ketone production, and promotes protein synthesis. Modern analogue insulins are engineered to act fast at meals (aspart, lispro) or flat and long as background (glargine, degludec), mimicking the natural pattern of a basal trickle plus mealtime bursts.
forms: Prefilled pens injected under the skin of the abdomen, thighs or buttocks, rotating sites; insulin pumps delivering rapid-acting insulin continuously; intravenous infusion in hospital; hybrid closed-loop systems with continuous glucose monitors
insulin.onset: Rapid-acting 10-20 minutes (peak 1-3 hours, lasts 3-5 hours); long-acting flat over 24 hours or more.

common: Hypoglycaemia (shaking, sweating, hunger, confusion): treat with 15-20 g fast sugar, recheck, then a snack
Weight gain
Lipohypertrophy (fatty lumps) at over-used injection sites, which absorb insulin erratically
Bruising, stinging
serious: Severe hypoglycaemia with seizure or coma, needing glucagon injection or intravenous glucose
Diabetic ketoacidosis if insulin is omitted in type 1 diabetes (never stop, even when not eating: adjust instead)
Hypokalaemia with intravenous infusion
Allergy (very rare with modern insulins)

cautions: Doses are individual and adjusted for food, activity, illness and glucose readings; errors in units are a major cause of harm ('units' written in full)
Sick-day rules: keep taking basal insulin, check glucose and ketones more often, drink fluids
Driving rules: check glucose before and every 2 hours; carry fast sugar
Store unopened insulin in the fridge; in use at room temperature for 4 weeks
insulin.monitoring: Fingerprick or continuous glucose monitoring several times daily; HbA1c every 3-6 months; annual eye, foot and kidney checks.

levothyroxine.name: Levothyroxine
levothyroxine.summary: Synthetic thyroid hormone (T4) that replaces what an underactive thyroid cannot make, restoring energy, weight and metabolism; the dose is set by regular TSH blood tests.
usedFor: Hypothyroidism from any cause (autoimmune, after surgery or radioiodine, congenital)
Suppressing TSH after thyroid cancer
Subclinical hypothyroidism when TSH is high, symptomatic, or in pregnancy
levothyroxine.howItWorks: A synthetic copy of thyroxine (T4), the hormone the thyroid normally releases. Tissues convert it to the active T3, which enters cell nuclei and switches on genes controlling metabolic rate, heat production, heart rate, gut motility, growth and brain development. Replacement restores the pituitary's TSH to normal, which is how the dose is tuned.
forms: Tablets 25, 50, 100 micrograms and oral solution, once daily on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast (or at bedtime)
levothyroxine.onset: Symptoms improve over weeks; TSH takes 6-8 weeks to settle after each dose change. Lifelong.

common: Few at the right dose; at too high a dose: palpitations, weight loss, sweating, anxiety, insomnia, diarrhoea (symptoms of hyperthyroidism)
Temporary hair loss in the first months
serious: Angina or atrial fibrillation if started too fast in the elderly or those with heart disease (start at 25 micrograms)
Bone loss and atrial fibrillation with long-term over-replacement
Adrenal crisis if given before untreated adrenal insufficiency is corrected

cautions: Absorption falls with calcium, iron, antacids, proton pump inhibitors, soya and coffee: separate by 4 hours
Dose often needs to rise in pregnancy (increase by 25-50% and check TSH promptly), and with oestrogen, enzyme inducers
Stay on the same brand where possible
Do not use for weight loss in people with normal thyroid function
levothyroxine.monitoring: TSH 6-8 weeks after starting or changing dose, then yearly once stable.

salbutamol.name: Salbutamol
salbutamol.summary: The blue reliever inhaler: a short-acting beta-2 agonist that opens the airways within minutes to relieve asthma and COPD symptoms during an attack or before exercise.
usedFor: Relief of wheeze and breathlessness in asthma and COPD ('reliever')
Before exercise in exercise-induced asthma
Nebulised or intravenous in severe asthma attacks and COPD flares
Lowering high potassium in emergencies (nebulised)
salbutamol.howItWorks: Stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors on the smooth muscle wrapped around the bronchi. This raises cyclic AMP inside the muscle cells, relaxing them within minutes so the airways widen and air moves more freely. It relieves the narrowing but does nothing for the underlying inflammation, which is why needing it more than twice a week signals poorly controlled asthma and the need for a preventer.
forms: Pressurised metered-dose inhaler 100 micrograms per puff (best with a spacer), dry powder inhaler, nebuliser solution, tablets and syrup (rarely), intravenous
salbutamol.onset: Within 5 minutes, peak 15-30 minutes, lasts 4-6 hours.

common: Fine tremor, fast heartbeat, palpitations, headache
Feeling shaky or restless; muscle cramps
serious: Low potassium with high doses (with steroids, diuretics, theophylline)
Arrhythmias in people with heart disease at high doses
Paradoxical bronchospasm (rare); over-reliance masking worsening asthma, linked to asthma deaths

cautions: Using more than three canisters a year, or needing it daily, means the asthma plan needs review
Anti-inflammatory reliever (budesonide-formoterol) is now preferred as the sole reliever in many guidelines
Inhaler technique matters: slow deep breath, hold for 10 seconds; spacers for children and during attacks
Beta blockers antagonise the effect
salbutamol.monitoring: Peak flow and symptom diary; frequency of use as a marker of control.

inhaled-corticosteroids.name: Inhaled corticosteroids
inhaled-corticosteroids.summary: The preventer inhalers of asthma: low doses of steroid delivered straight into the airways damp down inflammation so attacks become rarer and milder.
inhaled-corticosteroids.class: Inhaled glucocorticoid (with or without a long-acting beta-2 agonist)
usedFor: The cornerstone of asthma treatment: daily to prevent attacks and control symptoms
COPD with frequent exacerbations and high blood eosinophils, combined with long-acting bronchodilators
Combined inhalers with formoterol used as both preventer and reliever (MART regimens)
inhaled-corticosteroids.howItWorks: Steroid molecules deposited on the airway lining diffuse into cells and bind glucocorticoid receptors, which move to the nucleus and switch off the genes for inflammatory cytokines, reduce eosinophils and mast cells, and shrink mucosal swelling and mucus. Inhaling delivers a tiny dose straight to the airways, so the whole-body effects of steroid tablets are largely avoided. Benefit builds over days to weeks and depends on daily use.

inhaled-corticosteroids.onset: Symptoms improve over 1-2 weeks; full effect at 4-8 weeks.

common: Oral thrush and hoarse voice (rinse the mouth and use a spacer)
Sore throat, cough on inhaling
serious: Pneumonia risk in COPD at higher doses
At high doses long term: adrenal suppression, reduced bone density, cataract and glaucoma, easy bruising, a small effect on growth in children

Long-acting beta agonists must never be used alone in asthma without a steroid
Carry a steroid card at high doses; check bone density if on high dose for years
Technique check at every review
inhaled-corticosteroids.monitoring: Symptom control, reliever use, peak flow; growth in children; annual review.

omeprazole.name: Omeprazole
omeprazole.summary: A proton pump inhibitor that switches off acid production in the stomach, healing ulcers and reflux oesophagitis and protecting the stomach from anti-inflammatory drugs.
usedFor: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and its complications (oesophagitis, Barrett oesophagus)
Healing stomach and duodenal ulcers; part of H. pylori eradication triple therapy
Protecting the stomach in people on NSAIDs, aspirin or anticoagulants at ulcer risk
Bleeding ulcers (intravenous), Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
omeprazole.howItWorks: Irreversibly blocks the hydrogen-potassium ATPase, the 'proton pump' in the parietal cells of the stomach lining that secretes acid as the final step of every stimulus. Because the pump is disabled rather than the signals, acid falls by over 90%, and new pumps must be made before secretion recovers, so the effect outlasts the drug's short half-life. Given 30-60 minutes before breakfast, when pumps are most active.

Acute interstitial nephritis and, rarely, subacute cutaneous lupus

cautions: Use the lowest effective dose and review long-term use; rebound acid hypersecretion for a few weeks after stopping

omeprazole.understand: Omeprazole switches off the acid pumps in the cells of your stomach lining, so far less acid is made. With less acid, ulcers can heal, the oesophagus is no longer burned by reflux, and the stomach is protected from anti-inflammatory painkillers.
omeprazole.mechanismDetail: Omeprazole is a substituted benzimidazole prodrug. Absorbed from gastro-resistant granules, it concentrates in the acidic secretory canaliculi of gastric parietal cells, where it is protonated and converted to a sulfenamide that forms covalent disulphide bonds with cysteines on the H+/K+ ATPase, inhibiting the pump irreversibly. Because the pump is the final step of acid secretion, basal and stimulated acid output fall by more than 90%; secretion recovers only as new pumps are synthesised (half-life of pump turnover about 50 hours), so once-daily dosing before breakfast gives a sustained effect despite a plasma half-life of about an hour. Omeprazole is metabolised by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 and inhibits CYP2C19, reducing activation of clopidogrel and raising levels of some other drugs. Long-term acid suppression raises gastrin, alters absorption of magnesium, calcium, iron and vitamin B12, and changes the gut microbiome.

amoxicillin.name: Amoxicillin
amoxicillin.summary: A widely used penicillin antibiotic that kills bacteria by breaking their cell walls, prescribed for chest, ear, sinus, dental and some urinary infections and as part of Helicobacter pylori treatment; useless against viruses and dangerous only in true penicillin allergy.
usedFor: Chest infections and community-acquired pneumonia
Ear, sinus and throat infections caused by bacteria
Dental infections; H. pylori eradication (with a PPI and clarithromycin)
Urinary infections use nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim; skin infections flucloxacillin; atypical pneumonia doxycycline or clarithromycin
amoxicillin.howItWorks: Binds the penicillin-binding proteins that bacteria use to cross-link the peptidoglycan of their cell wall. Growing bacteria with a weakened wall burst under their own osmotic pressure. Human cells have no cell wall, which is why penicillins are so selective. amoxicillin.onset: Improvement within 48-72 hours; the full course is decided by the infection, not by symptoms.

serious: Anaphylaxis in true penicillin allergy (about 1 in 10,000 courses); most reported 'penicillin allergies' are not true allergy and can be safely delabelled

losartan.understand: Losartan blocks the action of angiotensin II, a hormone that narrows blood vessels and makes the body hold on to salt and water. With the hormone blocked, vessels relax and blood pressure falls, and the heart and kidneys are put under less strain.
losartan.mechanismDetail: Losartan and its more potent active metabolite (EXP3174) are selective, competitive antagonists at the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor. Because ACE is not inhibited, bradykinin is not accumulated and cough and angioedema are much less frequent than with ACE inhibitors. lisinopril.understand: Lisinopril stops your body making angiotensin II, a hormone that tightens blood vessels and makes the kidneys hold on to salt and water. Without it, vessels relax and the heart pumps against less resistance, so blood pressure falls and a weak heart has an easier job.
lisinopril.mechanismDetail: Lisinopril is a lysine analogue of enalaprilat that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (kininase II) directly without needing hepatic activation. Reduced angiotensin II lowers arteriolar tone, aldosterone secretion, sodium retention and sympathetic drive, and dilates the efferent glomerular arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria. Accumulation of bradykinin contributes to vasodilation and to cough and angioedema. In heart failure the fall in afterload and preload and the interruption of neurohormonal activation improve symptoms and survival; after myocardial infarction, early treatment limits ventricular remodelling. Lisinopril is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so exposure rises as eGFR falls and doses are reduced accordingly.

warnings.text: US labelling carries a boxed warning on fetal toxicity: stop lisinopril as soon as pregnancy is detected, because drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system injure and can kill the developing fetus.

Angioedema of the face, lips, tongue, glottis or larynx can occur at any time during treatment and may be fatal if the airway is involved; the risk is higher in people of Black African origin and with a history of angioedema. Intestinal angioedema presents as abdominal pain.

Kidney function can deteriorate, particularly with renovascular disease, heart failure, dehydration or NSAIDs; check creatinine and potassium before and 1-2 weeks after starting and after dose increases.

First-dose hypotension: a marked fall in blood pressure can follow the first dose in people on diuretics, on a low-salt diet, dehydrated or with heart failure; treatment is started at a low dose, sometimes with the diuretic paused.
Sick-day guidance: during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever with dehydration, UK information advises pausing lisinopril temporarily to protect the kidneys, restarting when eating and drinking normally.
Dizziness is common at the start; do not drive, cycle or use machinery until it has settled.

rosuvastatin.name: Rosuvastatin
rosuvastatin.summary: A high-intensity statin that lowers LDL cholesterol by more, milligram for milligram, than any other statin, used to prevent heart attacks and strokes when atorvastatin is not tolerated or not enough; the dose is limited by kidney function, ethnicity and interacting drugs.
usedFor: Lowering LDL cholesterol to prevent cardiovascular disease, as an alternative high-intensity statin to atorvastatin

rosuvastatin.howItWorks: Like atorvastatin it blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls cholesterol production in the liver, so the liver takes more LDL out of the blood. Rosuvastatin is the most potent statin by weight (5-10 mg gives a similar LDL reduction to 20-40 mg of atorvastatin), is water-soluble, and is barely metabolised by the liver's CYP enzymes, so it has fewer interactions with antibiotics and antifungals; instead its levels depend on transporters and on the kidney, which is why doses are capped in kidney impairment, in people of Asian ancestry and with ciclosporin or some HIV medicines.
forms: Tablets 5, 10, 20 and 40 mg once daily at any time of day; the 40 mg dose is for specialist use only
rosuvastatin.onset: LDL cholesterol falls within a week and reaches its maximum by four weeks. Taken lifelong.

common: Muscle aches (as with other statins, most reported aches also occur on placebo)

rosuvastatin.understand: Rosuvastatin blocks the enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol, so the liver takes more LDL cholesterol out of your blood. Lower LDL means less build-up in artery walls and a lower risk of heart attack and stroke.
rosuvastatin.mechanismDetail: Rosuvastatin is a hydrophilic, hepatoselective HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor taken into hepatocytes by OATP1B1. It reduces cholesterol synthesis, upregulates LDL receptors and lowers LDL cholesterol by about 45-63% across the 5-40 mg range, with larger HDL increases than other statins. Only about 10% is metabolised (mainly CYP2C9, negligibly CYP3A4), so macrolides and azole antifungals have little effect; exposure is instead raised by OATP1B1 and BCRP inhibitors (ciclosporin, gemfibrozil, some protease inhibitors) and by reduced renal function, and is about twofold higher in people of Asian ancestry because of transporter polymorphisms, hence the dose caps. High doses can cause dose-related proteinuria of tubular origin.

azithromycin.name: Azithromycin
azithromycin.summary: A macrolide antibiotic that stops bacteria making proteins, given as a short course (often three days) for chest, ear, sinus, skin and sexually transmitted infections and as an alternative in penicillin allergy; long-lasting in tissues, with cautions about heart rhythm and interactions.
usedFor: Community-acquired pneumonia and chest infections, particularly in penicillin allergy or when atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) are suspected
Ear, sinus, throat and skin infections in penicillin allergy
Chlamydia and some other sexually transmitted infections (single dose)
Long-term prophylaxis to reduce exacerbations in COPD and bronchiectasis, under specialist supervision (unlicensed use)
azithromycin.howItWorks: Binds to the bacterial ribosome (the 50S subunit) and blocks the tunnel through which new proteins leave, so the bacterium cannot make the proteins it needs to grow. Human ribosomes are built differently and are not affected. Azithromycin is concentrated inside cells, particularly white cells, which carry it to sites of infection, and it lingers in tissues for days after the last dose, which is why courses are short. Because it barely interferes with the liver's drug-metabolising enzymes, it has fewer interactions than erythromycin and clarithromycin.
forms: Capsules and tablets 250 and 500 mg, oral suspension; usually 500 mg once daily for 3 days, or a single 1 g dose for chlamydia; intravenous infusion in hospital
azithromycin.onset: Improvement expected within 2-3 days; tissue levels persist for 5-7 days after a 3-day course.

azithromycin.understand: Azithromycin stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to grow and multiply. Your immune system then clears the weakened bacteria. It builds up inside cells and stays in the body for days, so a course can be as short as three days.
azithromycin.mechanismDetail: Azithromycin is an azalide macrolide that binds reversibly to the 23S rRNA of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit within the peptide exit tunnel, blocking translocation and elongation of the nascent polypeptide; the effect is mainly bacteriostatic, bactericidal against some organisms at high concentrations. It achieves intracellular and tissue concentrations many times those in plasma, is delivered by phagocytes to infected tissue and has a tissue half-life of 2-4 days, allowing 3- to 5-day courses and single-dose regimens. Its spectrum includes streptococci, Haemophilus, Moraxella, atypical respiratory pathogens (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, Legionella), Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycobacterium avium complex; pneumococcal macrolide resistance is common in some regions. Unlike erythromycin and clarithromycin it is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4, but it inhibits P-glycoprotein (raising digoxin levels) and, like all macrolides, can prolong the QT interval. Long-term low-dose use in COPD and bronchiectasis works partly through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects.
